newsitem.title: GERMANY: German steel workers protest over merger plan.
newsitem.headline: German steel workers protest over merger plan.

text.p: Thousands of German steel workers protested on Wednesday at the prospect of a huge corporate merger between Krupp and Thyssen they fear could mean thousands of job losses in Germany's coal-and-steel heartland.

Over 6,000 angry steel workers downed tools and met at the vast Thyssen steelworks on the edge of the western city of Duisburg before marching to a hall in the city centre for an address by Thyssen Stahl chairman Ekkehard Schulz.

Schulz told the workers Thyssen planned to talk with Krupp about forming a joint steel group that would avoid a full-blown takeover. But workers said thousands of jobs would still be at risk and vowed to continue their protest action.
"It seems like the deal has already been done behind closed doors," said steel worker Werner Blaha, who has worked at Thyssen for 23 years.
"We should march to Bonn just like the miners," he said, referring to three days of miners' protests that succeeded in securing concessions from the government over its plans to cut coal subsidies.
Steel workers stopped work on Tuesday after they heard German industry giant Krupp planned a hostile takeover bid for Thyssen AG.
Outside the 10 entrances of the main Thyssen plant, workers lit coal fires in braziers to keep warm during their round-the-clock vigil.
"We were really surprised by the news that thousands of us could lose our jobs," said Hans-Dieter Schynetzek. "And when we're out, we've got no chances with over four million unemployed in Germany".

Protesters plastered banners on the gates of the plant, reading: "A future instead of job losses" and "Cromme and Deutsche Bank make Germany sick", referring to Krupp chairman Gerhard Cromme and Deutsche Bank's support for his planned bid.
Production remained at a standstill for the second day, but pungent smoke continued to belch from over 20 chimneys at the Thyssen plant as a skeleton staff tended blast furnaces.

The head of Thyssen Stahl works council, Dieter Kroll, said work would probably start again soon. He told a news conference the works council would meet on Wednesday afternoon to decide on their next move.
Asked if this meant the spontaneous walk-out would end, Kroll told a gathering of Thyssen Stahl workers in Duisburg, "Yes, I think so."
He said there would still be a protest gathering of workers as planned on Friday, which would be held jointly with Krupp workers.
Kroll said the new deal was better than a hostile takeover because it only concerned the Thyssen steel business.
"We need the facts before us before we can decide on our position," he said. "The problems won't just be wiped off the table. We are watching this process critically."
"I still can't believe that Krupp could try to take over Thyssen. That's like David taking Goliath," Kroll said.
But he said he thought over 5,000 jobs could be threatened at Krupp and said if a deal reached in eight days was unsatisfactory workers would not hesitate to strike again.
"People are afraid and they are unsure," Kroll said.
Earlier, Krupp and Thyssen said they planned eight days of meetings to develop a common plan to create a jointly-owned steel company.
Should those talks fail, the two companies would return to the starting blocks and Krupp would probably renew its offer to Thyssen shareholders.
